newsitem.title: USA: Some heart attack victims can benefit from drug.
newsitem.headline: Some heart attack victims can benefit from drug.

text.p: Men and women who have had heart attacks and have average cholesterol levels can significantly reduce their risk of another heart attack if they take the anti-cholesterol drug pravastatin, according to a study in Thursday's New England Journal of Medicine.
The finding suggests that pravastatin and other anti-cholesterol drugs can benefit more people than now use the medications.
The finding could create a broader market for such drugs in an era when most doctors believe that cholestrol levels in people who eat a typical Western diet are too high.

The five-year study involved 4,159 volunteers in the United States and Canada. All had average cholesterol levels and all had suffered heart attacks. Half received a placebo. The rest got pravastatin, which is sold under the brand name Pravachol by Bristol-Myers Squibb.

Team leader Dr. Frank Sacks of Brigham and Women's Hospital in Boston and his colleagues found that when people taking pravastatin were compared to the placebo recipients, their heart attack rate was 25 percent lower. In addition, their risk of stroke was cut by 31 percent.

In some catetories, the benefits were less clear. Although 38 placebo recipients had fatal heart attacks compared with 24 who got pravastatin, the difference was not big enough to be statistically significant. Fewer pravastatin recipients also died from all types of heart disease, but not enough to be statistically significant either.
The drug worked best when the initial cholesterol levels were highest. The more the drug reduced cholesterol counts, the greater the benefit.

Sacks and his colleagues found that when the level of one type of cholesterol -- low density lipoprotein or LDL -- ranged from 150 to 175, the drug cut the risk of heart attack or stroke by 35 percent. When the LDL levels were 125 to 150, pravastatin treatment reduced the risk by 25 percent. But below the 125 level, there was no apparent benefit.
Cholesterol levels are measured in milligrams per deciliter of blood.

"The study gives new importance to cholesterol-lowering therapy" because it cut the heart attack rate "in patients with cholesterol levels of less than 240 milligrams per deciliter," the Sacks team concluded.
If 1,000 heart attack patients with typical cholesterol levels got the drug, 150 new heart attacks or strokes would be prevented, they calculated.

When cholesterol-lowering drugs came on the market, there was concern that reducing cholesterol levels might open the door to cancer. The Sacks study found no link between pravastatin and cancer, with one exception. The researchers noted a "surprising" increase in breast cancer among women taking the drug.
While only one placebo recipient got breast cancer (and she had suffered with the disease previously), a dozen women in the pravastatin group developed it.
